title: The Wendigo
author: Algernon Blackwood
written: Out of Blackwood's years in Canada in the 1890s, and written in the run of tales that followed The Willows
setting: The bush north of Rat Portage in late October: a lake called Fifty Island Water, two days from the railway by canoe, with the first snow already down
lengthNote: Eight numbered sections, about 22,000 words, most of it two men in a tent and one set of footprints
openingLine: A considerable number of hunting parties were out that year without finding so much as a fresh trail; for the moose were uncommonly shy, and the various Nimrods returned to the bosoms of their respective families with the best excuses the facts of their imaginations could suggest.
summary: A moose-hunting party splits up, and a divinity student is sent off with a French-Canadian guide who does not want to go where they are going. In the night the guide smells something, weeps, and runs into the bush calling about his burning feet of fire. What is left behind is a set of tracks that begin as a man's and stop being one. The rest of the story is a psychologist explaining it all away while it happens to him too, and it ends with a thing walking into camp that the party's Indian cook does not stay to look at twice.
referenceStyle: section number, following the text the Astor edition is set from

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Wendigo (eBook 10897)
sourceText.note: The text the Astor edition's reading pages are set from, in eight sections. Blackwood's period spellings and the guides' written-out speech are kept; the story's terms for the Indigenous people of the region are of 1910 and are not reproduced in the quotations here.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Three years after The Willows, from the Canadian years Blackwood spent farming, reporting and going hungry.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: In The Lost Valley and Other Stories.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two days out, one night, and a long argument about what happened.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: The windigo of Ojibwe and Cree tradition, used by an English writer from the outside; the edition's notes set out the difference.

structure.label: Sections I-II
structure.title: A bad season, and a guide who does not want to go
structure.summary: Blackwood assembles five men with five different ways of explaining things: a Scottish psychologist who has written a book on collective hallucination, his nephew who is training for the ministry, two guides, and an Indian cook. The party splits, and Défago takes Simpson towards a lake he has reasons for avoiding that he does not give.

scenes.title: No fresh trail
scenes.summary: A season with no moose in it, and a doctor who comes home with something better than a trophy.

scenes.title: Défago
scenes.summary: A guide who sings in the canoe, knows the bush better than anyone, and has fits of melancholy nobody asks about.

scenes.title: Dividing the party
scenes.summary: Simpson goes with Défago towards Fifty Island Water; his uncle and Hank take the other direction.

structure.label: Sections III-IV
structure.title: The camp, and something on the far side of the canvas
structure.summary: They make camp on the lake, and the guide's nerve goes. He smells something on the air, cannot say what, and by nightfall he is frightened of the dark in a country he has worked in all his life. Simpson, who is twenty-something and reads everything as a spiritual exercise, notices and does not understand.

scenes.title: Fifty Island Water
scenes.summary: A lake that answers exactly to the description, and a guide who stops talking when they reach it.

scenes.title: The smell
scenes.summary: Faint, pungent, wrong for a forest — the odour Simpson will spend the rest of his life failing to describe.

scenes.title: The night
scenes.summary: Weeping in the tent, a man pressed against the canvas, and a voice outside calling his name.

structure.label: Section V
structure.title: He goes
structure.summary: Défago is called out of the tent by something that uses his name, and goes at a speed no man runs. What Simpson hears as the sound recedes is the story's most famous sentence, and it comes down out of the sky rather than along the ground.

scenes.title: Out of the tent
scenes.summary: The guide leaves in his stockinged feet, at a pace that takes him out of earshot in seconds.

scenes.title: Fiery height
scenes.summary: The cry about burning feet of fire, heard once, from above, and then silence over the whole wilderness.

structure.label: Section VI
structure.title: Two sets of prints, and one of them changes
structure.summary: Alone, in snow, Simpson follows what is left. Défago's prints run beside marks that are not a moose's and not a bear's, and as the trail goes on the distance between the man's footfalls grows until it can no longer be walked. Then his prints begin to resemble the other set.

scenes.title: The other track
scenes.summary: Big, round, ample, with no pointed outline: nothing in the bush leaves that.

scenes.title: The lengthening stride
scenes.summary: The gap between prints widening past any possible step, and the snow between them untouched.

scenes.title: The change
scenes.summary: The man's tracks losing their shape and taking on the other's — the moment the story stops being a disappearance.

structure.label: Sections VII-VIII
structure.title: The doctor explains, and the thing walks in
structure.summary: The party reunites and Cathcart sets out the rational account: suggestion, hysteria, a legend planted in a young mind by a superstitious guide. While he is still explaining, something comes into the firelight that answers to Défago's name and does not answer to anything else. The last pages give the facts of his death, the cook's flight, and no explanation at all.

scenes.title: Collective hallucination
scenes.summary: The doctor's theory, offered with real intelligence and no effect whatever on what happens next.

scenes.title: What came to the fire
scenes.summary: A shape that talks about moss and fire, and that Hank swears at until it goes.

scenes.title: Défago, afterwards
scenes.summary: A man found in the bush who lives a few weeks, eats moss, and complains that his feet burn.

scenes.title: Punk leaves
scenes.summary: The cook smells something on the air, walks three days without stopping, and never comes back.

characters.name: Simpson
characters.role: Cathcart's nephew, a divinity student on his first trip into the bush
characters.summary: Young, devout, entirely unprepared, and the only member of the party who sees the whole thing. His training gives him a vocabulary for awe and none at all for what is in front of him, and his honesty about that is what makes the account usable: he reports his terror as data rather than dressing it up.
characters.clue: Follows a trail alone in the snow and keeps measuring the distance between the footprints.

characters.name: Joseph Défago
characters.role: A French-Canadian guide, the best woodsman in the party
characters.summary: Cheerful in a canoe, subject to fits of gloom nobody enquires about, and frightened of one particular lake. Blackwood makes him competent first and terrified second, so that his collapse is a fact about the place rather than about his character. What comes back wearing his name is the story's worst moment.
characters.clue: Goes into the bush in his stockinged feet, and afterwards complains that his feet burn like fire.

characters.name: Dr Cathcart
characters.role: A psychologist from Aberdeen, author of a book on collective hallucination
characters.summary: He arrives with the explanation already written and spends the story applying it: suggestion, hysteria, a legend planted in an impressionable mind. He is never made a fool of — his reasoning is good and his nerve holds — but the narrator notes drily that this particular case never made it into his book.
characters.clue: Left one experience out of his own book because he had played too intimate a part in it.

characters.name: Hank Davis
characters.role: The other guide, and Défago's old partner
characters.summary: Profane, practical and the only man who talks about the Wendigo as a thing you might meet rather than a story you might hear. He blames himself for talking his friend into the trip, and he is the one who swears at the figure by the fire until it leaves.
characters.clue: Says there is no misunderstanding it, because it calls you by name.

characters.name: Punk
characters.role: The party's cook, an Indian who keeps the base camp
characters.summary: He has almost no lines and the story's clearest judgement. He recognises the smell before anyone else, and when the shape walks in he leaves, covering three days' travel without stopping. Blackwood gives the one man with inherited knowledge of the country no argument and no explanation — only the decision to go.
characters.clue: Cleaning fish when the thing comes into camp, and on the trail home within the minute.

relationships.label: recognises, and will not stay near

characters.name: The Wendigo
characters.role: Whatever calls Défago out of the tent
characters.summary: Never described except by its effects: a smell, a voice that knows your name, tracks that are not an animal's, and a man who comes back changed. Blackwood borrows an Algonquian figure and strips it of the cultural setting that gives it meaning, which is both the source of the story's power and the fairest charge against it.
characters.clue: Its mark is a smell like lions and a stride no legs could take.

themes.name: Country that does not know you are there
themes.summary: The bush in this story is not malevolent; it is simply larger than the people in it, and the story keeps giving the exact distances — two days from the railway, a lake with fifty islands, three days' walk home.
themes.development: It is beautiful in the canoe chapters, indifferent by the camp, and by the tracking section it is a surface that records what happened without commenting on it.

themes.name: One man, one trail, no help
themes.summary: The party is divided in the second section so that the worst night can happen with only one witness, and Simpson spends the middle of the story entirely alone.
themes.development: Being alone is what makes his testimony doubtful, and the doubt is what the last three sections are about.

themes.name: A divinity student in the bush
themes.summary: Simpson is training for the ministry and reaches instinctively for prayer, and the story neither mocks him nor rewards him. His religion gives him a way to feel awe and no way to act on it.
themes.development: He prays in the tent and tracks in the snow, and by the end his account has lost its religious vocabulary altogether.

themes.name: Four kinds of explanation
themes.summary: A psychologist, a theology student, a bushman and a cook each know something about what is happening, and the story lets them contradict each other without appointing a winner.
themes.development: Cathcart's hallucination theory is the most sophisticated and the least useful; the cook's, which is never argued, is the one the plot obeys.

themes.name: Tracks in snow
themes.summary: Everything supernatural in the story arrives as a physical trace — prints, a smell, a burnt smell on the skin, a distance between footfalls that can be paced out and measured.
themes.development: The trail is the story's argument: it starts as evidence of a man, becomes evidence of something else, and its most frightening stretch is the part where the two sets converge.

themes.name: What the doctor tells himself
themes.summary: Cathcart is the reader's proxy, and Blackwood treats him fairly: his explanation covers most of the facts, and he keeps offering it while the thing he is explaining is in the firelight with him.
themes.development: The narrator's one dry remark — that this case never appeared in his book on Collective Hallucination — is all the verdict the story delivers.

themes.name: A borrowed figure
themes.summary: The Wendigo comes from Ojibwe and Cree tradition, where it carries meanings about famine, winter and the danger of appetite. Blackwood takes the name and the terror and leaves the meaning behind, and his Indigenous character is given knowledge but almost no speech.
themes.development: The story's frame treats Indigenous belief as evidence of something real and its Indigenous characters as atmosphere, and modern readers have to hold both facts at once.

techniques.name: The bush, measured
techniques.definition: Setting described with the precision of someone who has worked in it.
techniques.inThisBook: Distances, portages, the weight of a canoe, the behaviour of moose in a bad season: Blackwood had lived this country, and the accuracy is what makes the one impossible detail land.

techniques.name: The trail as text
techniques.definition: A physical record that the characters and the reader read together.
techniques.inThisBook: Hank draws a bull's hoof on birch bark so Simpson can compare. From then on the snow is a document, and the horror is a matter of shape and spacing.

techniques.name: The cry that comes back
techniques.definition: A line repeated at intervals, each time in a different mouth.
techniques.inThisBook: The burning feet of fire are heard from the sky in section five, from the figure at the fire later, and finally from a dying man in a bed. Each repetition takes something away from the possibility of hallucination.

techniques.name: Guides' speech written out
techniques.definition: Rendering pronunciation and idiom on the page.
techniques.inThisBook: Hank's swearing and clipped consonants set him against Cathcart's careful Aberdeen sentences, so that the argument about what happened is also an argument between two kinds of English.

techniques.name: The thing never shown
techniques.definition: Keeping the central figure off the page.
techniques.inThisBook: There is no description of the Wendigo anywhere in the story — only a smell, a voice, tracks, and what is left of a man. The reader assembles it and is responsible for the result.

techniques.name: Terror in the open
techniques.definition: The old machinery of dread moved out of doors.
techniques.inThisBook: A tent instead of a castle, snow instead of a crypt, and a guide instead of a servant. The pressure is gothic and the furniture is a canoe, a fire and a pair of moccasins.

techniques.name: A story with witnesses
techniques.definition: An account assembled afterwards from several people's testimony.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator sorts what Simpson said, what Hank admitted, what Cathcart would concede and what Punk contributed. The story is presented as a case file, which is precisely why the doctor's rejection of it matters.

quotations.text: A considerable number of hunting parties were out that year without finding so much as a fresh trail
quotations.context: The story's first sentence, on the season's bad hunting.
quotations.analysis: It opens on an absence, and on men going home with stories. The whole tale is about what one party brought back instead of a trophy, and the first line quietly puts the reader among people who exaggerate.

quotations.text: This particular story, however, found no mention in his book on Collective Hallucination
quotations.analysis: The rationalist is given his credentials and his one omission in the same sentence, on page one. Everything he says for the next eight sections is read against a fact the reader has been handed in advance.

quotations.text: the vagaries of the human mind
quotations.analysis: His subject is named before the case arrives, so his diagnosis is available from the start. Blackwood is playing fair: the psychological reading is offered by the text itself and not smuggled in.

quotations.text: the “odor of lions” is the phrase with which he usually sums it all up
quotations.context: Simpson, years later, still trying to describe the smell.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is wrong for a Canadian forest and that is the point — the nearest thing he can reach for is an animal from another continent. Blackwood repeats the phrase three times across the story, so a smell becomes the creature's signature.

quotations.text: Wendigo’s somewhere around, doin’ a bit of swift traveling
quotations.context: Hank, explaining the smell to Simpson early in the trip.
quotations.analysis: The name arrives casually, in a guide's idiom, as a piece of weather. Introducing the creature as workaday local knowledge rather than as revelation is what makes the later sections unbearable.

quotations.text: Oh! oh! This fiery height! Oh, my feet of fire! My burning feet of fire
quotations.context: Défago's voice, heard once from far above the camp.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted sentence Blackwood wrote, and it does two things at once: it tells the reader that the man is airborne, and it puts the pain of it in his own mouth. The exclamations are the only moment the prose loses its composure.

quotations.text: They were big, round, ample, and with no pointed outline as of sharp hoofs
quotations.context: Simpson examining the second set of prints in the snow.
quotations.analysis: Blackwood describes it by elimination: not a moose, not a caribou, not a bear. The adjectives are so neutral that they do the work of a scream, because the one thing the reader wants — what made them — is exactly what the sentence refuses.

quotations.text: These mysterious writings left in the snow by the unknown creature that had lured a human being away from safety
quotations.analysis: Writings, not tracks. Once the snow is a text the story's method is clear: Simpson is reading, the reader is reading over his shoulder, and the horror is a problem of interpretation rather than of sight.

quotations.text: several Indians had “seen the Wendigo” along the shores of Fifty Island Water
quotations.context: Hank finally explaining why Défago did not want to hunt there.
quotations.analysis: The information that would have changed everything arrives after the event, from the man who talked his friend into going. Blackwood puts local knowledge in quotation marks, which is both the story's method and the fairest charge against it.

quotations.text: for the Wendigo is simply the Call of the Wild personified, which some natures hear to their own destruction
quotations.context: Cathcart, breaking a long silence by the fire.
quotations.analysis: The doctor's neatest formulation, offered to fill a pause rather than because he believes it settles anything. It is a good line, it is almost certainly wrong, and the story gives it to the cleverest man present.

quotations.text: It calls you by name right ’nough
quotations.context: Hank's answer to the doctor's theory.
quotations.analysis: Seven words that dispose of a paragraph of psychology. The bushman does not argue with the theory; he adds a detail it cannot accommodate, and the detail is the one Simpson heard outside the tent.

quotations.text: But Défago surely had already told you all these details of the Wendigo legend, my dear fellow
quotations.context: Cathcart pressing his nephew on where the images came from.
quotations.analysis: The suggestion theory, put politely and in the form of a question. It is the explanation most readers would reach for, and Blackwood has it stated by a professional so that nobody can accuse the story of ducking it.

quotations.text: It’s a moss-eater, is the Wendigo
quotations.context: Hank, after the figure at the fire has gone.
quotations.analysis: The detail is grotesque rather than grand, and that is why it convinces: nobody inventing a terror puts moss in it. It also sets up the last section, where a man in a bed pulls wads of it out of his cheeks.

quotations.context: What the recovered Défago says about himself before he dies.
quotations.analysis: Hank's phrase comes back out of the mouth of the man it was used about, with an idiot smile attached. The repetition is the story's proof: the same words in two places nobody could have coordinated.

quotations.text: bereft of mind, memory and soul, had gone with it
quotations.context: The narrator's summary of what became of the guide.
quotations.analysis: Three nouns, in order of increasing loss, and then the flat verb. For a story that refuses to describe its monster, this is as close as it comes to saying what the monster does.

quotations.text: The terror of a whole race drove him
quotations.context: Punk covering three days' travel without stopping, after the thing walks into camp.
quotations.analysis: The cook is the only person in the story who acts on what he knows, and the narrator explains him in a single sentence that is also the story's most uncomfortable. Inherited knowledge is treated as evidence and its holder is given no voice at all.

quotations.context: The last sentence of the story.
quotations.analysis: It closes on the local phrase, in quotation marks, refusing to translate it into the doctor's language or the student's. After eight sections of competing explanations the story ends by using the one it started with and declining to gloss it.

timeline.label: Blackwood born in Kent
timeline.detail: Into the evangelical household whose certainties his supernatural fiction keeps testing.

timeline.label: Blackwood emigrates to Canada
timeline.detail: He emigrated at twenty, failed at dairy farming and hotel-keeping near Toronto, and learned the bush he writes about here.

timeline.label: Blackwood a struggling reporter in New York
timeline.detail: Years as a reporter and model, often destitute; the wilderness in his fiction is remembered from real weeks of it.

timeline.label: Blackwood returns to England
timeline.detail: He returned at thirty and began writing the stories that used the country he had left.

timeline.label: Blackwood's The Willows published
timeline.detail: The Danube story that made his reputation and set the pattern this one follows.

timeline.label: The Wendigo published
timeline.detail: In The Lost Valley and Other Stories, the collection that consolidated the reputation.

timeline.label: Lovecraft praises Blackwood in Supernatural Horror in Literature
timeline.detail: Supernatural Horror in Literature praises Blackwood above all his contemporaries and singles out the Canadian tales.

timeline.label: Blackwood begins broadcasting his stories on the BBC
timeline.detail: Blackwood began broadcasting his stories and became one of the first voices people knew from the wireless.

timeline.label: Algernon Blackwood dies
timeline.detail: He died at eighty-two, with the Canadian stories still the work most anthologised.

places.name: Rat Portage, now Kenora
places.note: The railway town the hunting party outfits from.

places.name: Lake of the Woods
places.note: The island-scattered water the story's Fifty Island Water is drawn from.

places.name: Toronto
places.note: Where Blackwood farmed, kept a hotel and failed at both in the early 1890s.

places.name: Montreal
places.note: The Quebec world Défago has strayed from, and the French-Canadian bush trade it supplied.

places.name: Aberdeen
places.note: Dr Cathcart's city, and the source of the story's rationalism.

criticalViews.summary: Tighter than The Willows, with a stronger cast, a real plot and the most frightening sentence he ever wrote; the tracking section is often called the finest sustained passage in English weird fiction.
criticalViews.counter: It gives away more than The Willows does. Once the figure has a name, a diet and a set of symptoms, it has become a creature — and creatures are less frightening than the unnameable.

criticalViews.summary: The psychological reading is given to the most intelligent character and stated at full strength, so the supernatural has to earn its place against it.
criticalViews.counter: The narrator tips the scale on the first page by telling us the case never appeared in Cathcart's book, and the last section supplies physical corroboration no hallucination could leave.

criticalViews.summary: The windigo belongs to Algonquian peoples and carries meanings about famine, winter and cannibal appetite; Blackwood takes the name and the dread and discards the context, and his one Indigenous character is given knowledge, no speech, and an exit.
criticalViews.counter: The story does place the authority with that knowledge — the cook is right and the doctor is wrong — and the edition's notes set out the tradition the fiction borrows from, which is the least a reader is owed.

essayQuestions.question: How does the story handle the competition between explanations?
essayQuestions.focus: Rationalism, testimony and who the reader believes
plan: Set out the four positions: Cathcart's psychology, Simpson's religion, Hank's bush lore, Punk's silence.
Show the narrator's early hint about the book on Collective Hallucination and what it does to the reading.
Examine Cathcart's suggestion theory at full strength, and what it fails to cover.
Use the repetition of the burning-feet cry and the moss as physical corroboration.
Decide whether the story adjudicates or simply outlasts the argument.

essayQuestions.question: What makes the tracking section frightening?
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, pacing and the reader's own inference
plan: Describe the set-up: Hank's drawing on birch bark, so the reader can compare prints too.
Follow the sequence — two sets, an impossible stride, the change in the man's own prints.
Note how little is asserted and how much is measured.
Compare it with the moment of the cry, where the story does assert something.
Argue for why inference frightens more reliably than description.

essayQuestions.question: Is the story's use of the windigo defensible?
essayQuestions.focus: Borrowed belief, and who is allowed to speak
plan: Establish what the windigo means in Algonquian tradition and what Blackwood keeps of it.
Look at how the story reports Indigenous knowledge: in quotation marks, at second hand, after the event.
Weigh the fact that this knowledge is the only account the plot vindicates.
Set Punk's three-day walk against his near-total silence in the text.
Conclude on what a modern edition owes a reader here.

discussionQuestions: Cathcart is clever, brave and wrong. Does the story treat him fairly?
The Wendigo is never described. Did you picture it anyway, and from what?
Why does Blackwood give the guide a French-Canadian name and a Scottish doctor an Aberdeen one?
Punk walks three days without stopping and says nothing. What would change if he had a speech?
Is the moss a mistake — too concrete, too odd — or the detail that makes it real?
The story ends on a phrase in quotation marks. Why not translate it?

related.why: Its companion, three years earlier: the same method on the Danube, with nothing named at all.
The phrase Cathcart reaches for by the fire, and the novel that had made it a fixed idea seven years before.
The same northern bush treated as a place with rules, by a writer who thought it could be understood.
The older story of a pursuit across a frozen landscape by something that will not be outrun.
The other case where the rational explanation is offered inside the text and refuses to settle it.
